title: IPO Base
teaches: The IPO base as we trade it: a new issue's first rest under its own IPO high, light volume on the pullbacks, never bought on the listing day or in the listing week, the buy is the trade through the IPO high at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

steps: KRMN listed in February 2025, a defence name in a hot theme. Its first rest sits under the IPO high, 57.32.

walkthroughs.title: VIK, June 2024: short, shallow, and the trail
steps: VIK listed in May 2024 and rested just 2.0 weeks under its IPO high, only 9% deep. Short and shallow.

June 28 it clears the IPO high on 2.8 times volume. Buy at market, 33.38. Stop just under the day's low, 32.62.

walkthroughs.title: MA, January 2007: the textbook stop-out

Next session it trades down to 10.18 and takes the stop. It never showed a gain. Take the loss and move on.

questions.why: Our card gives the top grade for breakout-day volume of at least 1.4 times the base's average. Multiply: 1,200,000 times 1.4 is 1,680,000. Volume raises the grade. It is not needed for the setup to count. The listing week is left out of that average. IBD's test is 40% above the 50-day average, and many new issues have yet to trade that long. Our card compares with the base's own sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Measure breakout volume against the base's own sessions, not the listing week.
questions.simple: It takes 1,680,000 shares, because the top grade needs at least 1.4 times the base's average of 1,200,000 a day.

reasons: a computed key
the 1.4 times line is a proposed card gate that D-006 may turn into a grade cue

choices: 1,680,000 shares
2,880,000 shares
2,600,000 shares

wrong.16,800,000 shares: That is ten times too many. A decimal slip.
wrong.2,880,000 shares: That adds the base again on top of 1.4 times.
wrong.2,600,000 shares: Added 1.4 million to the average instead of multiplying by 1.4.

questions.q: Does that close back in the base change your plan?
choices: Sell it all, the breakout failed
Sell half, it slipped back in
Hold, the stop is still the exit
Hold, and lower the stop for room
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit. A close back inside the base is a warning, something to watch, not a sell. You set that stop with a clear head before you bought, and it already caps the loss. Selling on a wobble just swaps your plan for a feeling. If it keeps sinking, the stop takes you out. If it turns, you're still in. My stop is my stop.
questions.lesson_line: Back in the base is a warning. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Sell it all, the breakout failed: It hasn't failed until the stop goes. A close back in the base is a warning, not an exit.
wrong.Sell half, it slipped back in: There's no half-sell for slipping back. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Hold, and lower the stop for room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lowering it turns a planned loss into a bigger one.

questions.story: You bought the IPO-high break at 19.53. Two days later it closes back inside the base, still above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold. The stop was set before the buy and already caps the loss, so a warning alone isn't a reason to sell.

deeper.trap: MarketSmith India would rather not see a breakout slip back into the base, and that's fair as a warning. But a warning asks you to look harder, not to sell on a hunch. Decide the exit before the buy, then let the stop or the trail do the work.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, A4: the stop is the exit

questions.q: Which breakout day has A+ volume?
choices: Day A only
Day B only
Both days
Neither day
questions.answer: Day B only
questions.why: Day B only. A+ volume is 2 times or more the 10-day average, or the highest volume of any session after the listing day. Neither day is the heaviest since listing, so the 10-day average decides. Day B is at 2.2x and Day A at 1.5x. Both clear the 1.4x trigger line, so that line does not separate them. Grading stays a judgment call; this is the volume cue only.
questions.lesson_line: The A+ volume cue is 2 times the 10-day average. The 1.4x line is only the minimum.

wrong.Day A only: Day A is at 1.5x its 10-day average. A+ volume starts at 2 times that average.
wrong.Both days: Both clear the 1.4x trigger line, but that line is only the minimum. Day A stops short of 2 times its 10-day average.
wrong.Neither day: Day B is at 2.2x its 10-day average, over the 2 times that A+ volume asks for.

questions.story: Same base, two breakout days. Day A trades 1.6x the base's average volume and 1.5x its 10-day average. Day B trades 1.8x the base's average and 2.2x its 10-day average. Neither is the heaviest day since listing.
questions.simple: Day B. It trades 2.2x its 10-day average, and A+ volume starts at 2 times that average.

reasons: the A+ volume line is a proposed card cue
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, wait until the report is out
Yes, it's a clean, tight base
Yes, but only at half size
Wait a day, then buy before it
questions.answer: No, wait until the report is out
questions.why: Wait until the report's out. We don't make a new buy in the 3 sessions before earnings, and this one reports in 2. A report can gap a stock right through your stop overnight. Your small planned loss turns into a big one, and no stop order can prevent that. New issues report their first quarter soon after listing, so check the date before you plan the trade. If the base holds up after the report, it'll give you another trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date on every new issue. Inside 3 sessions, no new buy.

wrong.Yes, it's a clean, tight base: A clean base doesn't change the earnings window. No new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: Half size still gaps through the stop. The rule is no new buy in that window.
wrong.Wait a day, then buy before it: Tomorrow is still inside the 3 sessions. Wait until after the report.

questions.story: The base is tight under the IPO high and breaks out this morning. The first quarterly report is in 2 sessions.
questions.simple: Wait. A report can gap the stock right past your stop overnight, so no new buys this close to it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B22
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: A stock listed 6 weeks ago rests under its high. Which card applies?
choices: The cup with handle card
The IPO base card
The flat base card
questions.answer: The IPO base card
questions.why: The IPO base card. The listing date decides: an IPO base is a young stock's first rest under its post-listing high inside its first year.
questions.lesson_line: Many IPO bases look like cups. The listing date decides which card applies.

wrong.The cup with handle card: A cup needs a stock with a trading history. A stock listed 6 weeks ago has none.
wrong.The flat base card: A flat base is for a seasoned leader, not a stock listed 6 weeks ago.

questions.q: How do you judge this rest?
choices: An IPO base, it's a young stock
A flat base, by its shape
A VCP, by its tightening
Nothing, there's no 200-day
questions.answer: An IPO base, it's a young stock
questions.why: An IPO base. AXTA listed 68 sessions before the breakout, and this is its first rest under its high. Plenty of IPO bases look like cups or flat bases. The shape doesn't decide, the listing date does. A stock this young has no track record, so we judge it the way we judge new issues. And no 200-day isn't a reason to skip it. It's just too young to have one.
questions.lesson_line: Shape doesn't decide it. A young stock's first rest is an IPO base.

wrong.A flat base, by its shape: It looks flat, but a young stock's first rest is judged as an IPO base. Age decides, not shape.
wrong.A VCP, by its tightening: Even if it tightens, tightening inside an IPO base just raises the grade. A young stock's first rest is still an IPO base.
wrong.Nothing, there's no 200-day: 68 sessions is too young for a 200-day. That doesn't cancel the setup.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. Look at the rest under the high. This stock listed 68 sessions before the breakout and has rested 6.4 weeks, 12% deep, under its post-listing high. It is the first rest, and its numbers could pass for a flat base.
questions.simple: An IPO base. A young stock's first rest gets judged as an IPO base, whatever shape it takes.

deeper.counter: Shape isn't the label. While the stock is young, a rest that looks like a flat base is judged as an IPO base. Past its first year, it's a regular base and gets judged on those rules.

reasons: the window is a held decision, D-002
fixed before: story rewritten

questions.q: Which setup is it?
choices: A VCP, since the swings shrink
A bull flag, as it is a pause
An IPO base; tightening is a cue
A failed breakout, retesting
questions.answer: An IPO base; tightening is a cue
questions.why: An IPO base, and the tightening is only a grade cue. The stock is four months old and resting under its post-listing high, so the listing date decides. A young listing has no 200-day and one rest. Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue, not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue. It does not change the card.

wrong.A VCP, since the swings shrink: Tightening inside an IPO base is a grade cue, not a VCP. A young listing has no 200-day and one rest.
wrong.A failed breakout, retesting: Nothing has closed above the high, so there has been no breakout to fail. It is a first rest under the high.
wrong.A bull flag, as it is a pause: The story has no sharp run before the rest. It is a first rest under the post-listing high, and on a stock this young that is an IPO base.

questions.story: A stock listed four months ago rests under its highest price since listing for the first time. Nothing has closed above it. The weekly swings inside the rest get smaller each week.
questions.simple: It is an IPO base, because the stock is young and resting under its own high, and shrinking swings only help the grade.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line; the 200-day rule for young stocks is held (D-034)

questions.q: How does this base look?
choices: Weak; the V leaves no right side
Strong; buyers took it back
Strong; it is near the high
Weak; it must close above it
questions.answer: Weak; the V leaves no right side
questions.why: Weak. A fast V is a poor sign. The price ran from the low back to within 5% of the pivot in 5 sessions or fewer, with no pause. Here it went from 25% under the high to within 3% in four sessions. That leaves no right side to judge.
questions.lesson_line: A fast V straight into the pivot is a poor sign. It has no right side.

wrong.Strong; buyers took it back: A quick rebound looks bullish, but with no pause there is no quiet right side to judge.
wrong.Strong; it is near the high: Being near the high is only the end point. With no pause there was no right side to judge.
wrong.Weak; it must close above it: The trigger is a trade through the IPO high, not a close above it. It is weak because the V leaves no right side.

questions.story: A new issue drops 25% off its IPO high. Then in four sessions, with no pause, it climbs back within 3% of that high.
questions.simple: Weak. The price shot back up to the pivot in a few days with no pause, so there is no right side to judge.

deeper.trap: Being back near the high looks bullish. But a V in a few sessions leaves nothing to judge: no quiet pullbacks, no proof the sellers are done. A base earns its buy by resting, not by racing.

reasons: the V line is a proposed card line
the card also lists a fast V as a B- cue (c35): owner to rule which wins

questions.q: Your normal size doesn't fit that stop. What do you do?
choices: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low
Move the stop up so the size fits
Full size, it's only one trade
Risk more to keep my usual size
questions.answer: Fewer shares, stop stays at the low
questions.why: Fewer shares. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, 28.70. That's where the chart says you're wrong. From 30.09 that's 4.6%, wider than the 1-3% I like, but under 5% I'll take it. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. Pull the stop up just to fit more shares and normal noise takes you out. So buy fewer, and a hit at the stop costs the planned amount. NAVN took the stop the next session. Small, planned, done.
questions.lesson_line: Never pull the stop in to fit the size. Cut the shares, or wait for a tighter trigger.

wrong.Move the stop up so the size fits: That puts the stop inside normal noise. The honest stop stays, and the shares come down.
wrong.Full size, it's only one trade: Full size on a wider stop means a bigger loss than you planned. Every trade gets the same risk.
wrong.Risk more to keep my usual size: That's how losses creep up. The risk stays put and the share count changes.

questions.story: You bought the break of the IPO high at 30.09. The low of the day puts your stop at 28.70.
questions.simple: Fewer shares. The stop stays where the chart says you're wrong, and the smaller size keeps the loss as planned.

reasons: wide-stop sizing is tied to the held decision D-005
rests on the owner's rulebook, A3 and A5
fixed before: variety rewrite 2026-11-10

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Your call, sell some or hold it
Sell part, the gap past 3R says so
Sell it all, a gap is a gift
Wait 30 minutes before doing anything
questions.answer: Your call, sell some or hold it
questions.why: It's your call. The open at 62.00 is past 3R at 61.53, but a gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling some locks in the jump right there. Holding keeps the whole position for a bigger 3, 5 or 7 day push. It's day 4, so a sale isn't early. I very rarely sell on day 1, and day 3 is the earliest I like. Some days I'd sell a piece into a gap like this. Some days I hold.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your sell level isn't an order. It's a decision, and it's yours.

wrong.Sell part, the gap past 3R says so: Selling part into a gap is one choice. It isn't a rule that 3R forces on you.
wrong.Sell it all, a gap is a gift: Too much at once. If you sell, sell a piece and keep the rest working.
wrong.Wait 30 minutes before doing anything: Nothing makes you wait. You can act right at the open if that's your call.

questions.story: You bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05. On day 4 the stock opens at 62.00, above 3R at 61.53.
questions.simple: Your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell, so sell a piece into it or hold for a bigger push.

deeper.example: Gaps skip levels. The open is above 3R and it's day 4, so selling a piece is fair. Holding for a longer push is fair too. The gap is a chance to decide, not a rule to follow.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, F63 and B19
computed level, 61.53 is given in the story

questions.q: You've got a few clean new-issue bases on your list. What kind of market do you most want behind them?
choices: A market turning up after a correction
Late in a long run, with IPOs everywhere
A market that's still falling hard
The first days of a new market drop
questions.answer: A market turning up after a correction
questions.why: Coming off a correction. New issues get sold hardest when the market corrects. They tend to lead once it turns and buyers come back. That's a cue I watch, not a rule. The flip side: be careful late in a long run when the IPO calendar is packed. A crowded calendar that late is a warning sign to me.
questions.lesson_line: New issues lead best out of a correction. A crowded calendar late in a run is a warning.

wrong.Late in a long run, with IPOs everywhere: That's when I'm careful. A crowded IPO calendar late in a long advance is a warning.
wrong.A market that's still falling hard: Worst spot there is. New issues get hit hardest in a correction.
wrong.The first days of a new market drop: New issues are the first to get hit when the market stumbles.

questions.simple: Right after a correction, when the market turns up, because new issues fall hardest when it's weak.

reasons: rests on the card's cue line
key was the longest choice before

questions.q: We scanned 57 IPO base breakouts. Most of them hit the stop before they ever reached 3R.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Right, 36 of the 57 got stopped before 3R. That's normal for breakouts, and it's why the stop matters so much. The scan used a fixed stop and no sells. Read it as a base rate, not a call on your next trade. You lose small most of the time. The few that work can run past 5R and pay for the rest. Size from the stop, keep every loss small, and let the winners do the work.
questions.lesson_line: Most breakouts stop out. Small losses and a few big winners is the whole game.
questions.simple: True. Most hit the stop first, so we keep each loss small and let the few winners pay for them.

deeper.trap: Do not read a base rate as a promise. In the same scan 26.3% reached 3R and 17.5% reached 5R before the stop. The plan lives on small losses and on letting the few winners run.

reasons: a number from our own scan that changes when the scan is rerun
one source family, the research dossier

questions.q: $100,000 account, 0.5% risk. How many shares do you buy?
questions.answer: 225 shares
questions.why: 225 shares. Your risk is 100,000 times 0.5%, so $500. Your risk a share is 54.72 minus 52.50, which is 2.22. 500 divided by 2.22 comes to just over 225, and you round down. Never up. Now if BSY hits the stop, you lose the planned $500 and no more. In real life you check the position cap next, and the smaller number wins.
questions.lesson_line: Risk dollars divided by risk a share, rounded down. That's your size.
questions.simple: 225 shares. Size off the stop, so if it hits you lose the 500 you planned and no more.

deeper.trap: Round up and that one extra share puts you a little over the $500 you planned. Round down, every time, so the risk never goes past your limit.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, shares from the stop)

choices: 450 shares
500 shares
2,252 shares
225 shares

wrong.500 shares: That's the risk dollars read as shares. Divide by the risk a share.
wrong.2,252 shares: A decimal slip. That's ten times the risk you planned.

questions.story: You bought the IPO-high break at 54.72. Your stop is a few cents under the low of the day, at 52.50. That's 2.22 of risk a share. Leave the position cap aside for this one.

questions.q: This new issue is a fast mover. What do you trail what's left with?
choices: The 9 EMA
The 20 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
questions.answer: The 9 EMA
questions.why: The 9 EMA. Fast movers ride their short line. When one closes under the 9, that's the first real sign the run is done. Trail a fast one with a slower line and you hand back a big chunk before you're out. So you sell what's left on a close below the 9 EMA. Steadier movers get the 20. New issues are fast movers more often than not.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Close below it and what's left goes.

wrong.The 50-day: Way too slow for a fast mover. You'd give back most of the run.
wrong.The 200-day: A young stock may not even have a 200-day. And it's far too slow for a trail.
wrong.The 20 EMA: That's for a steadier mover. A fast one gives back too much before it closes under the 20.

questions.simple: The 9 EMA. A fast mover hugs its quick line, so a close under that line is your first sign the run is over.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, E52

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 62.64 with the stop at 60.76.

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Sell it and free up the money
Sell half and hold the rest
Hold it, the base was clean
Move the stop up to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free up the money
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days in and still under 1R, it goes. A stock that's done nothing has shown you no buyers. Meanwhile that money could be in the next setup that's actually moving. A clean base doesn't buy it more time. And breakeven isn't the move here. The stop comes up to breakeven from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell, not at 0.4R.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and still under 1R, it's out. Money is for trades that work.

wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: Breakeven comes from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. At 0.4R, it's the time stop.
wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The time stop sells the whole trade. We sell part into strength, not into a stall.
wrong.Hold it, the base was clean: The base doesn't matter now. Under 1R after 10 trading days, it's out.

questions.story: You bought an IPO breakout 10 trading days ago. It has drifted sideways and is up only 0.4R.
questions.simple: Sell it. A stalled trade ties up money that could be working in a better setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, C33

questions.q: Do you take the fourth one?
choices: Skip it, three tries is the week's max
Take it, every trigger is a new trade
Take it at half size to be safe
Skip it, and stay away for a month
questions.answer: Skip it, three tries is the week's max
questions.why: Skip it. One stock gets 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, and you've used the week's three. After three stop-outs the itch is to win it back. That's how a few small planned losses turn into one big one. Every re-buy is a new trade with its own stop, sure. But the limit comes first. If it sets up again next week, it's fair game.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week, six a month. Then let it go.

wrong.Take it at half size to be safe: The limit is on tries, not size. A fourth try is over it at any size.
wrong.Take it, every trigger is a new trade: A new trigger is a new trade, but one stock still gets 3 tries a week.
wrong.Skip it, and stay away for a month: The limit is 3 a week and 6 a month. It's not a month-long ban.

questions.story: Three times this week you bought the same new issue's breakout and the stop took you out. A fourth trigger fires on Friday morning.
questions.simple: Skip it. You've used this week's tries, and chasing a stock to win it back is how small losses grow.

deeper.trap: Each stop-out was a planned loss. The pull is to try once more to win it back. The limit says no. Move on to the next setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, B21 and E56

questions.q: After a stop-out we can buy the same stock again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, with its own stop and every rule. At most 3 tries in a week.
questions.lesson_line: A new buy is a new trade: new trigger, new stop, every rule again.

questions.q: You've sold your first piece into a push. What's the plan for the rest?
choices: Sell more on strength, then trail
Sell it all at 5R and move on
Add more at 5R if it acts well
Hold all of it, no more sells
questions.answer: Sell more on strength, then trail
questions.why: Sell more into strength, then trail what's left. The first sell is a judgment, into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or around 5 to 10R. Later sells work the same way. When it pushes again, I sell more into it while buyers are paying up. Whatever's left rides the 9 or 20 EMA until it closes below. That's how one winner pays for a lot of small losses.
questions.lesson_line: Sell into strength, then trail what's left.

wrong.Sell it all at 5R and move on: Selling it all at one mark cuts the winner short. Keep a piece on the trail.
wrong.Add more at 5R if it acts well: That's a new buy, not a plan for what's left. What's left gets sold into strength and trailed.
wrong.Hold all of it, no more sells: Then a later push goes by with nothing sold. Selling into strength locks some of it in.

questions.simple: Sell more into the next push, then trail the rest. That locks in gains and keeps the winner working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, B19)

questions.q: What do you do with your position?
choices: Sell a big part into the gap
Add a little on the gap up
Hold it all, trail the 9 EMA
Raise the stop and sell nothing
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the gap
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. You're in a climax run on your own long, the final rush. Huge volume on another gap up is when buyers are most eager. That's the best time to sell to them. How big a part is your call. Then the rest trails the 9 EMA, and a close below it ends it. I'd rather sell into a burst like this than give it back on the way down.
questions.lesson_line: When your new issue goes vertical on huge volume, sell a big part into it.

wrong.Add a little on the gap up: A climax is the worst time to add. This is when you sell to the eager buyers.
wrong.Raise the stop and sell nothing: Raising the stop is fine, but on a climax you sell a big part, not just tighten up.
wrong.Hold it all, trail the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA handles what's left. A climax is your chance to sell a big part first.

questions.story: Your new-issue long has gone almost straight up for weeks. Today it gaps up again on huge volume.
questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst. A climax is the final rush, so you sell to the eager buyers.

deeper.trap: A big part is not all of it. How much you sell is a judgment. The rest still trails the 9 EMA for a fast mover, and a close below it is the exit.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, 'yes but depends')

questions.q: What do you make of this base going into tomorrow?
choices: Weak, it sank under the first open
Fine, it's clearing its IPO high
Weak, the first day opened too high
Fine, it's a new issue's first base
questions.answer: Weak, it sank under the first open
questions.why: Weak. SPOT opened its first day at 165.90, and this base sank all the way to 135.51. That's 18% under the price the first buyers paid. In a young stock I want the base holding above the IPO price. Sink under it and a lot of early buyers are losing money. Plenty of them will sell into any bounce just to get out. SPOT cleared its high anyway, and the breakout went nowhere, 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A young stock's base should hold above its IPO price. Sink under it and early buyers want out.

wrong.Fine, it's clearing its IPO high: Clearing the high is the trigger, not the test. The problem is the base under it.
wrong.Weak, the first day opened too high: A strong open isn't the issue. The issue is the base sinking under it later.
wrong.Fine, it's a new issue's first base: That's what makes it an IPO base. It still has to hold above the first open, and this one didn't.

questions.story: A direct listing opened its first day at 165.90. Its first base sank as low as 135.51. Tomorrow it trades through its IPO high.
questions.simple: Weak. The base sank under the first day's open, so early buyers were underwater and ready to sell.

deeper.trap: Don't judge the floor by the breakout alone. A stock can clear its IPO high after the base has already broken its floor. IBD and MarketSmith India both want the base above the IPO price. On a direct listing, the first open stands in for it.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-057: which price counts as the IPO price)
fixed before

questions.q: How do you judge this one?
choices: A regular base, on its own rules
An IPO base, it listed recently
Skip it, it's too old to be one
An IPO base, it lacks a 200-day
questions.answer: A regular base, on its own rules
questions.why: A regular base. CAVA broke out 318 sessions after listing, well past its first year. By then it has a track record and a 200-day, so the IPO base idea doesn't fit anymore. The shelf itself is clean, 3.6 weeks and 14% deep, breaking out on 2.2x volume. Nothing wrong with that. It just gets judged as a flat base or a cup, by those rules.
questions.lesson_line: Past the first year, an IPO base is just a base.

wrong.An IPO base, it lacks a 200-day: At 318 sessions it has a 200-day. Age decides here, and it's past a year.
wrong.An IPO base, it listed recently: 318 sessions is more than a year. It's not a young stock anymore.
wrong.Skip it, it's too old to be one: Too old for an IPO base, not too old to trade. Judge it as a regular base.

questions.story: The day before the breakout. Look at the shelf under the high. A clean 3.6-week, 14% shelf breaks out on 2.2x volume the next day. The breakout comes 318 sessions after listing.
questions.simple: A regular base. After its first year a stock has a track record, so it's judged like any other base.

deeper.example: CAVA had a clean 3.6-week, 14% shelf on 2.2x volume, 318 sessions after listing. The shelf was fine. It was simply too old to call an IPO base.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-002: the first-year window)

questions.q: How do you grade this breakout?
choices: Weak, buyers didn't show up
Strong, spin-offs tend to run
Strong, the base was tight
Weak, the base was too deep
questions.answer: Weak, buyers didn't show up
questions.why: Weak. NWSA cleared its high on 0.75x the base's average volume. That's below an ordinary day in the base. When a breakout is real, buyers show up in size and volume jumps. Here they didn't. For us volume raises the grade, it doesn't make or break the setup. So it grades lower and gets a smaller size. It isn't a ban. The best it did was 0.82R.
questions.lesson_line: No volume on the breakout means no demand. It lowers the grade, it doesn't kill the setup.

wrong.Strong, spin-offs tend to run: The label doesn't make a breakout strong. The volume on the day does.
wrong.Strong, the base was tight: A tight base helps. But the breakout day still needs buyers, and they weren't there.
wrong.Weak, the base was too deep: 10% is shallow. Most IPO bases correct less than 20%, so depth isn't the problem.

questions.story: The breakout day. Look at the volume on the day against the base. A spin-off listed in June. A 6-week, 10% base at the high breaks out today on 0.75x the base's average volume.
questions.simple: Weak. Volume was below the base's normal, so buyers didn't show up, and that lowers the grade.

deeper.trap: IBD wants heavy volume on the breakout day and week. We treat it as a grade cue. NWSA's 0.75x day graded weak, and the breakout went nowhere.

reasons: rests on held decisions (D-006: volume as a gate or a cue; D-054: spin-offs)

questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: The stop should have been wider
Nothing; the stop did its job
We should have skipped the breakout
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop did its job
questions.why: Nothing went wrong. The honest stop was 6.7% away and sized for it. The trade reached 0.6R and fell to the stop four sessions later. That is a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A wide honest stop is sized in shares. When it hits, the loss is the plan.

wrong.The stop should have been wider: Widening the stop is a named mistake. It only grows the loss.
wrong.We should have skipped the breakout: Every rule passed, and the size was set from the stop. Skipping it afterwards is hindsight.

questions.story: MDB: a 20% base on 1.8x volume. The honest stop is 6.7% under the fill. It reaches 0.6R, then falls to the stop four sessions later.

questions.q: The filter says Yellow. How do you handle this breakout?
choices: Smaller size and fewer positions
Full risk, the base is clean
Only take A+ setups for now
Mostly cash, no new longs
questions.answer: Smaller size and fewer positions
questions.why: Smaller and fewer. Yellow means the market isn't fully behind breakouts, so I take less risk and fewer trades. Green is full risk, Orange is A+ only, and Red is mostly cash. New issues get hit hardest when the market wobbles, so the reading matters even more here. APTV is the lesson. Clean bases, a 2.8x breakout, and it still stopped out twice in a flat 2012 market.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market first, then the chart. Yellow means smaller and fewer.

wrong.Full risk, the base is clean: Full risk is Green. A clean base doesn't make the market Green.
wrong.Only take A+ setups for now: That's Orange. Yellow still trades, just smaller and fewer.
wrong.Mostly cash, no new longs: That's Red. In Yellow you trade, but smaller and fewer.

questions.story: Our market filter goes Green, Yellow, Orange, Red, strongest to weakest. It's been a flat year, and it reads Yellow. This new issue's first breakout stopped out. Tomorrow it breaks out of a second clean base.
questions.simple: Smaller and fewer. The market isn't fully behind breakouts, and weak markets hit new issues hardest.

deeper.trap: A clean base doesn't make the market Green. APTV's two clean-looking failures came in a flat 2012 market. Read the market first, then the chart.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65 market reading)

questions.q: Was the setup wrong?
choices: No; the loss is planned
Yes; the base was too short
Yes; the stop was too tight
questions.answer: No; the loss is planned
questions.why: No. Every rule passed and the stop was set before the buy. NAVN broke out on 2.1x volume, closed near the high, and fell through the stop the next session.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can still lose. The stop is the cost of finding out.

wrong.Yes; the base was too short: A short base is fine for a new issue. The loss is not proof the rule failed.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop was the honest one. Widening it after the fact only grows the loss.

questions.story: NAVN: a 2-week, 7% shelf at the IPO high breaks out on 2.1x volume and closes near its high. Next session it falls through the 4.6% stop.

questions.q: Same chart otherwise. Which one would you rather own?
choices: The 12% one, sellers did less
The 33% one, more room to run
Neither, depth tells you nothing
The 33% one, it shook out more
questions.answer: The 12% one, sellers did less
questions.why: The 12% base. A shallow base means sellers couldn't push it down much, and the stock held near its highs. That's strength. Most IPO bases correct less than 20%, so 33% is a deep one, with more damage to repair. Depth is one thing I weigh, not the whole grade. But all else equal, I want the one that barely gave anything back.
questions.lesson_line: All else equal, take the shallow base. It gave back less.

wrong.The 33% one, more room to run: A deeper fall isn't a bonus. It's more damage to repair before the highs.
wrong.Neither, depth tells you nothing: Depth tells you how hard sellers hit it. Shallow is the healthier sign.
wrong.The 33% one, it shook out more: A deep drop isn't proof of a shakeout. Mostly it means sellers were in charge longer.

questions.story: Two IPO bases are otherwise similar. One is 12% deep. The other is 33% deep.
questions.simple: The 12% base. A shallow rest means sellers did less damage, and that's the healthier sign.

deeper.trap: Grading is a judgment, with no fixed checklist. Depth moves the grade. It doesn't decide it alone.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-055: the depth cap and grade lines)
fixed before

questions.q: This new issue grinds higher, slow and steady, late in its first year. What do you trail it with?
choices: The 20 EMA
The 9 EMA
The listing-day low
The 200-day
questions.answer: The 20 EMA
questions.why: The 20 EMA. A steady mover dips under the 9 all the time without the trend breaking. Trail it with the 9 and you get shaken out of a good trend. The 20 gives it room, and you sell what's left on a close below it. SABR was that kind of stock late in its first year. Fast movers get the 9, steady ones get the 20.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steady mover, 20 EMA.

wrong.The listing-day low: That's a level to know, not a trail. It doesn't move up with the stock.
wrong.The 9 EMA: That's for fast movers. A steady one dips under it and shakes you out.
wrong.The 200-day: Too slow to trail with, and a stock in its first year may not even have one.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA. A steady mover needs a bit more room, so the slower line keeps you in the trend.

questions.q: Do you buy it at the open?
choices: No, too stretched and past 4%
Yes, it cleared the IPO high
Yes, if I keep the stop tight
Not until it closes above the high
questions.answer: No, too stretched and past 4%
questions.why: No. It's past both lines. It opens 12% over the IPO high, and we don't pay more than 4% past the buy point. It's also 18% over its 9 EMA, and we skip anything more than 10% above it. Buy that and you're late to a move that already happened. Your stop still belongs back near the buy point, so the risk a share balloons and the size shrinks. Let it go and wait for the next setup.
questions.lesson_line: Too far past the pivot is a pass. Wait for the next setup.

wrong.Yes, it cleared the IPO high: Clearing the high is the trigger. The 4% limit and the stretch check still apply.
wrong.Yes, if I keep the stop tight: A tight stop up here sits in the noise. The honest stop is far below, and that kills the size.
wrong.Not until it closes above the high: We buy the trade through the trigger, not the close. The problem here is the stretch.

questions.story: A new issue gaps up and opens 12% above its IPO high. At the open it's 18% over its 9 EMA.
questions.simple: No. It's way past 4% over the pivot and over 10% above the 9 EMA, so you'd be late.

deeper.trap: A gap can look like a strong breakout and still be too late. The 4% chase limit and the 10% stretch limit are separate checks, and this entry fails both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, C29)
held decision D-017 on exceptions
fixed before

questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
choices: No, only a 5R winner holds through
Yes, the stop will protect me
Yes, 2R is enough cushion
Sell half, hold half through it
questions.answer: No, only a 5R winner holds through
questions.why: No, I'm out before the report. We hold through earnings only when the trade's up 5R, and this one's up 2R. A report can gap a stock straight through your stop overnight. The stop order won't save you there. It just fills at the open, wherever that is. Up 5R, you've got a real cushion to absorb a gap like that. At 2R you don't. Take the win and look again after the report.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R, you can hold through a report. Under that, be out.

wrong.Yes, the stop will protect me: A stop can't stop a gap. It fills at the open, well under your price.
wrong.Yes, 2R is enough cushion: One bad gap eats 2R and more. The bar is 5R.
wrong.Sell half, hold half through it: Half a position still takes the gap. Under 5R, be out.

questions.story: You hold an IPO winner that is up 2R. Its first report as a public company comes after the close tomorrow.
questions.simple: No. A report can gap right past your stop, and only a trade up 5R has room to take that.

deeper.trap: Do not mix up the two earnings rules. No new buys in the 3 days before a report is about entries. Holding through a report only if up 5R is about trades you already own. A new issue's first report can come soon after listing, so check the date.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
fixed before

questions.q: The chart's perfect. Do you trade it?
choices: Pass, too thin and too cheap
Take it, the chart is perfect
Take it at half size to be safe
Wait for the next report, then buy
questions.answer: Pass, too thin and too cheap
questions.why: Pass. We trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. At 7.40 and $3 million a day, this one fails both. A thin stock jumps on small orders. Your stop can fill way under where you set it, and selling in size moves the price against you. I wouldn't even keep it on the list. Perfect charts show up on thin stocks all the time. They're not for us.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect chart on a thin stock is still a pass.

wrong.Take it at half size to be safe: Half size doesn't fix a stop that can't fill. The floor is the same for every setup.
wrong.Take it, the chart is perfect: The floor comes before the chart. Thin stocks aren't even on our list.
wrong.Wait for the next report, then buy: The report isn't the problem. Price and volume are, and both fail the floor.

questions.story: A new issue trades at 7.40 and averages 3 million dollars a day. Its base and breakout both look perfect.
questions.simple: Pass. It's too cheap and too thin, so you couldn't get out clean when you need to.

deeper.trap: A perfect chart on a thin stock is a trap, not a bargain. We do not even watch illiquid stocks, and we never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)

questions.q: What's the move?
choices: Get out, the loss is past 2R
Hold, 52.40 is the new stop
Hold and wait for it to come back
Sell half and hold the rest
questions.answer: Get out, the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes decide. The low of that first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. But there's a ceiling. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're done. Here 2R is 2.74 a share, and you're down 5.02. Way past it. The ceiling is there so one bad gap can't turn a planned loss into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Hold, 52.40 is the new stop: That's only half the rule. The 30-minute low becomes the stop unless the loss is past 2R. It is.
wrong.Hold and wait for it to come back: Hoping isn't a plan. Past 2R, you're out.
wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The ceiling says get out, not trim. Half still carries the loss.

questions.story: You bought at 57.42 with the stop at 56.05, so 1R is 1.37 and 2R is 2.74 a share. The stock gaps down through the stop. The low of the first 30-minute bar is 52.40, 5.02 under your fill.
questions.simple: Get out. The gap took the loss past 2R, and the ceiling keeps one gap from becoming a big loss.

deeper.trap: The new-stop rule has a ceiling. Many people remember that the first 30-minute low becomes the stop and stop reading there. The ceiling is the part that matters in a deep gap: past 2R, get out. Do not wait for a recovery.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
computed key (the loss against 1R)
fixed before

questions.q: How does that earnings dip change things?
choices: Lowers the grade, the chart still leads
Nothing, the numbers don't matter here
It kills the setup and the grade
Lowers the grade, the numbers lead
questions.answer: Lowers the grade, the chart still leads
questions.why: It lowers the grade, but the chart still leads. I prefer growing sales and earnings, the latest quarter up year over year. Growth gives buyers a reason to keep holding a young company. Sales up and earnings down is a mixed quarter, so I grade it a notch lower and size it that way. It doesn't void a clean base. Chart first, numbers second.
questions.lesson_line: Growth helps the grade. The chart's still the boss.

wrong.Nothing, the numbers don't matter here: They count toward the grade. Falling earnings knock it down.
wrong.It kills the setup and the grade: Growth is a preference, not a gate. The chart comes first.
wrong.Lowers the grade, the numbers lead: The chart leads. The numbers move the grade, they don't run the show.

questions.story: A clean IPO base breaks out. Its latest quarter shows sales up but earnings down year over year. Our grade is our judgment of how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.
questions.simple: It lowers the grade. Growth gives buyers a reason to hold, but the chart still comes first.

deeper.trap: Don't turn a preference into a gate. Growing sales and earnings are preferred, and falling earnings lower the grade. A weak quarter doesn't void a clean base on its own.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D40 preference)
fixed before

questions.q: A new issue breaks out of a clean base. You cut your normal size just because it's a new listing.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: No special cut. We don't have a separate rule for new listings. The stop already does that job. A new issue that swings wide gets a wider stop, and a wider stop means fewer shares on the same risk. The grade does the rest. A+ gets sized up, and B- or lower gets sized down to 0.25% to 0.5% risk. So size it like any other trade, off the stop and the grade.
questions.lesson_line: No special IPO size. The stop and the grade set it.
questions.simple: False. The stop and the grade already set the size, so a new issue needs no extra cut.

deeper.trap: Don't invent a rule we don't have. A new issue gets no special size cut. The stop sets the share count, and the grade sets the risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E53, D38, E49)
held decision D-034

questions.q: Right before the breakout, a tight base goes quiet: small daily ranges and no big swings up or down.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Right. Tight means quiet. In the last few days before a breakout I want small ranges and closes stacked right on top of each other. Big jumps or drops in there mean the stock's still loose, with buyers and sellers still fighting over it. A big down day is as loose as a big up day. A quiet right side gives you a tight stop, and that makes the trade easy to manage.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is quiet. Wide swings on the right side mean it isn't ready.
questions.simple: True. Small ranges and no big swings mean the stock has settled, and that gives you a tight stop.

deeper.trap: Stockbee checks for no two 4% days, up or down, in the 5 days before the breakout. Count both directions. A big drop is as loose as a big jump.

reasons: proposed criteria-card line, backed by one practitioner

questions.q: Which right side is the best sign for an IPO base?
choices: Wide swings with heavy volume
A fast V straight into the pivot
Inside days on very low volume
A tight range down near the base low
questions.answer: Inside days on very low volume
questions.why: Inside days on very low volume, with weekly ranges under 10%. IBD described CBRE's three-week base as tight trading with weekly ranges of less than 10%. A fast V into the pivot leaves no right side to judge, and wide swings are a loose base.
questions.lesson_line: The best right side is quiet: inside days, low volume, tight weekly ranges.

wrong.Wide swings with heavy volume: That is a loose base, not a tight one.
wrong.A fast V straight into the pivot: That is a B- sign. The V leaves no right side to judge.
wrong.A tight range down near the base low: Tight is not enough. The base's last close should sit in the top half of its range, not near the low.

questions.simple: The best right side is quiet and tight, with inside days on very low volume and weekly ranges under 10%.

deeper.example: IBD's CBRE base. The buy point was 20.10, 10 cents above the left-side high. It was a three-week base with tight trading and weekly ranges of less than 10%.

reasons: proposed criteria-card line, backed by one IBD example

questions.q: The day before a breakout. Is this a first rest under the IPO high? Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; a tight rest under the high
Pass; a new issue cannot form a base
Pass; it has no 200-day
Take it; any rest under a high is fine
questions.answer: Take it; a tight rest under the high
questions.why: Take it. This is a 6.8-week, 22% deep first base under the IPO high, with the low held above the IPO open. It broke out the next day on 2.2x volume and reached 3R the day after. A young stock has no 200-day, so the IPO high is its landmark.
questions.lesson_line: Find the IPO high first. Then look for a quiet rest under it.

wrong.Pass; a new issue cannot form a base: IBD says to let a new issue build some trading history and wait for its first base. New issues do form bases.
wrong.Pass; it has no 200-day: A young stock has no 200-day yet. The IPO high and the IPO price are its landmarks.
wrong.Take it; any rest under a high is fine: Not any rest. It must be a first base under the IPO high with the low held above the IPO open, and the buy is a trade through the high.

questions.simple: Take it, because this is the stock's first tight rest under its IPO high, with the low held above the IPO open.

deeper.example: After the reveal: KRMN. Buy 57.42, stop 56.05 (2.4%), and 3R came the next day. Even so, 36 of the 57 scan hits were stopped before 3R. A clean base is a probability, not a promise.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-055: the 22% depth against a possible 20% cap)
key read from our own bars

questions.q: The day before it trades through its high. Does the base hold above the first day's open?
choices: Take it; the shelf is tight
Pass; the base sank under the first open
Take it; the volume is rising
questions.answer: Pass; the base sank under the first open
questions.why: Pass. The base low 135.51 sat under the IPO open 165.90, an 18% undercut. The breakout reached 0.0R. This is a direct listing and the chart begins on its first day.
questions.lesson_line: Compare the base low with the first day's open before you look at the breakout.

wrong.Take it; the shelf is tight: A tight shelf does not fix a floor that already broke.
wrong.Take it; the volume is rising: Volume is one sign. The base failed the floor first.

questions.q: Do you jump in?
choices: Check base, stop and size first
Buy half now, decide the rest later
Buy now before it runs away
Copy the post's entry, stop and size
questions.answer: Check base, stop and size first
questions.why: Not off a post. You do your own work first: the base, the stop, the size. You don't know where the poster's stop is, how big they are, or when they'll sell. Copy the trade and you've got no plan when it drops. Every buy I make has its entry, stop and size written down before the open. If it really is a good setup, it goes on tomorrow's list with your own plan.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert isn't a plan. Your entry, your stop, your size.

wrong.Buy half now, decide the rest later: Half a gamble is still a gamble. No stop and no plan, at any size.
wrong.Buy now before it runs away: No stop and no size means no plan. If it runs, it runs.
wrong.Copy the post's entry, stop and size: Their plan fits their account, not yours. Build your own.

questions.story: Someone posts that a new issue is breaking out right now. It wasn't on your plan for today.
questions.simple: Do your own check first. A post gives you no stop or size of your own, so you can't manage it.

deeper.trap: A post can be right and still not be your trade. If the stop isn't yours, the size isn't yours either, because the size comes from the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F66, D39)

questions.q: What is your call on the setup?
choices: Pass; Red means mostly cash
Buy it; it has relative strength
Buy a starter position
questions.answer: Pass; Red means mostly cash
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, and a Red reading ends the setup before the trigger. New issues are sold first when the market weakens.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits. Cash is a position.

wrong.Buy a starter position: A starter in a Red market is still a long. Mostly cash means mostly cash.
wrong.Buy it; it has relative strength: Relative strength does not cancel a Red market. New issues fall hardest.

questions.story: A textbook IPO base is one tick from its pivot. The market reading is Red and the indexes are breaking down.

questions.q: Which base would you rather take?
choices: Neither; volume does not matter
Base A: it shakes out weak hands
Base B: buyers show up when it rises
Whichever base has more volume
questions.answer: Base B: buyers show up when it rises
questions.why: Base B. Light volume on the pullbacks and heavy on the up days is the healthy pattern. On the right half, up-day volume should exceed down-day volume. Base A shows the reverse.
questions.lesson_line: Two bases can look alike. Volume on the right half tells them apart.

wrong.Neither; volume does not matter: Volume on the right half of the base matters. Up days should carry the heavy volume.
wrong.Base A: it shakes out weak hands: On the right half, up-day volume should exceed down-day volume. Base A shows the reverse.
wrong.Whichever base has more volume: Total volume hides the side. Heavy volume on down days is selling, and we look for it on up days.

questions.story: Two IPO bases have the same depth and length. In Base A the right-half down days carry the heavy volume. In Base B the up days do.
questions.simple: Base B, because buyers show up on the up days, while Base A has its heavy volume on the down days.

deeper.trap: Two bases with the same depth and length can still differ. Compare the volume on up-close days with the volume on down-close days on the right half. The shape of the price alone will not show it.

reasons: card line agrees with IBD, proposed gate

questions.q: What does the location tell you?
choices: A good sign; it lifts the grade
Nothing; the averages do not matter
It is stretched; skip the trade
A good sign; it replaces the trigger
questions.answer: A good sign; it lifts the grade
questions.why: A good sign, so it lifts the grade. The A+ location is above the IPO AVWAP and the rising 9 and 20 EMA. The IPO AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price anchored at the listing day. Sitting above the 9 EMA is normal, and we skip a long only when it is more than 10% above it.
questions.lesson_line: Above the IPO AVWAP and the rising short averages is the best location.

wrong.Nothing; the averages do not matter: Location is part of the grade. Above all three is the A+ version.
wrong.It is stretched; skip the trade: Stretched means more than 10% over the 9 EMA. At 4% over it, this is not stretched.
wrong.A good sign; it replaces the trigger: Location is a grade cue, not a trigger. The buy still needs a trade through the IPO high.

questions.story: A breakout candidate sits above its IPO AVWAP. It is also above its rising 9 and 20 EMA, and 4% over the 9 EMA.
questions.simple: A good sign, because sitting above the IPO AVWAP and the rising 9 and 20 EMA is the best location.

deeper.trap: Above the averages is a good place to be, not a reason to chase. Location is one grade cue. We still skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed grade cue

questions.q: Is your friend right?
choices: No, the usual exit plan works
Yes, sell all of it at 2R
Yes, take a small trim at 1R
No, but give it a wider stop
questions.answer: No, the usual exit plan works
questions.why: No. Same plan as every trade: entry, stop, trim, trail, advance. The stop sits a few cents under the low of the day and only moves up. The first sell is a judgment into a push, and I very rarely sell on day 1. Then the rest rides the trail. One plan is easier to follow when a new issue is whipping around. The stop already handles the extra risk.
questions.lesson_line: New issue or not, same plan. Entry, stop, trim, trail, advance.

wrong.Yes, sell all of it at 2R: Selling it all at 2R cuts every winner short. Sell into a push, then trail.
wrong.Yes, take a small trim at 1R: There's no 1R trim. The first sell is a judgment into a push, and day 3 is the earliest I like.
wrong.No, but give it a wider stop: The stop only moves up, never wider. It goes under the low of the day, like any setup.

questions.story: You buy an IPO base breakout. A friend says new issues need a different exit plan from every other setup.
questions.simple: No. One plan for every trade is easier to follow, and the stop already limits the loss.

deeper.trap: A friend's view isn't a rule. Plan every trade as Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail, Advance. We have no separate rule for new listings.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A12, E53)
held decision D-034

questions.q: Which card is it?
choices: No card; it is too old
The IPO base card
A regular base card, not the IPO base
questions.answer: A regular base card, not the IPO base
questions.why: A regular base card. The stock listed years ago and is far from its first year, so the IPO base card does not apply.
questions.lesson_line: An old stock gets an old stock's card. Do not force the IPO label.

wrong.The IPO base card: The IPO base card is for a young stock's first rest inside its first year.
wrong.No card; it is too old: Old stocks make bases too. They follow their own cards.

questions.story: A stock that listed several years ago builds a 6-week rest at its highs. It looks tight and clean.

questions.q: Is this an IPO base?
questions.story: Our chart only shows 30 sessions of history, with a neat rest under the high. The company listed six years ago.
choices: No, it first traded six years ago
Yes, the chart starts 30 sessions ago
Yes, any neat rest under a high counts
No, it needs an earnings report first
questions.answer: No, it first traded six years ago
questions.why: No. Age counts from the first day the stock traded, not from the first bar on our chart. This company has been public six years. A short chart just means we're missing data, not that the stock is new. Six years means a track record, so it gets judged as a regular base. Check the listing date in the app before you call anything an IPO base.
questions.lesson_line: Date the listing from the record, never from where the chart starts.

wrong.Yes, the chart starts 30 sessions ago: The chart's start isn't the listing. The company was public years before that bar.
wrong.Yes, any neat rest under a high counts: It also has to be a young stock, and age counts from the first trade.
wrong.No, it needs an earnings report first: Reports don't decide age. The first day of trading does.

questions.simple: No. Age counts from the first day of trading, so a short chart doesn't make a stock new.

reasons: one source: the criteria card (c46), a proposed line

questions.q: A $40 new issue averages 650,000 shares a day. What's the most shares you'll own of it?
questions.answer: 6,500 shares
questions.why: 6,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 650,000 is 6,500. Own more than that and getting out takes a real bite of a day's trading. You end up pushing the price down on yourself as you sell. That ceiling holds even when your stop math says you could buy more.
questions.lesson_line: 1% of the daily volume is the most I'll own, whatever the stop allows.
questions.simple: 6,500 shares. Stay under 1% of the daily volume so you can sell without pushing the price on yourself.

reasons: one cited fact only
a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

choices: 65,000 shares
650 shares
260,000 shares
6,500 shares

wrong.650 shares: A decimal slip. That's a tenth of the line.
wrong.260,000 shares: That's 1% of the dollar volume. The cap counts shares, not dollars.

questions.q: Your IPO breakout has a really tight stop, so the risk math gives a huge share count. You can own more than 1% of its daily volume.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: No. 1% of the daily volume is a ceiling, however tight the stop. A tight stop gives you more shares on the risk math, sure. But the volume cap is about getting out, not about risk. Own too much of a stock's daily trading and you can't sell without moving it on yourself. And a tight stop can't catch a gap. Take the smaller of the two numbers.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop sets the size from risk. It never lifts the volume cap.
questions.simple: False. The volume cap is about being able to get out, so a tight stop never lifts it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D42, A5)

questions.q: Which one do you want?
questions.story: Two IPO bases look alike: same depth, same volume, same shape on the right side. One sits in one of the strongest groups in the app's group ranking. The other's group ranks among the weakest.
choices: The one in the strongest group
The one in the weakest group
Either one, the group doesn't matter
The one whose group has more stocks
questions.answer: The one in the strongest group
questions.why: The one in the strong group. We buy leaders in the strongest groups. When a whole group is working, money is flowing into it, and a breakout there has more buyers behind it. A weak group is a headwind. Check where the group sits in the app's group ranking before you pick. Two equal charts, the group breaks the tie for me.
questions.lesson_line: Same chart, better group, better trade. Buy leaders in leading groups.

wrong.The one whose group has more stocks: Group size isn't the measure. Where the group ranks is.
wrong.The one in the weakest group: That's swimming against the current. We want leaders in the strongest groups.
wrong.Either one, the group doesn't matter: It matters. A leading group puts more buyers behind the breakout.

questions.simple: The one in the strongest group. A breakout there has more buyers behind it.

reasons: one source: the criteria card (c47), a proposed grade cue

questions.q: What does the location check ask of it?
questions.story: The day before the breakout, which comes 40 sessions after listing. It has no 50-day yet.
choices: The 9 and 20 EMA; the 50-day later
The 50-day, so wait until it has formed
The 200-day first, then the 20 EMA
No averages yet; judge the chart alone
questions.answer: The 9 and 20 EMA; the 50-day later
questions.why: The 9 and 20 EMA now. Our card asks for a close above the rising 9 and 20 EMA, and above the 50-day once it exists. At 40 sessions this stock has no 50-day yet, and a young listing has no 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A young stock is judged on the averages it has. The 50-day joins later.

wrong.The 50-day, so wait until it has formed: The 50-day is asked for only once it exists. A young stock does not have to wait for it.
wrong.No averages yet; judge the chart alone: At 40 sessions it already has a 9 EMA and a 20 EMA. Our card asks for a close above both.
wrong.The 200-day first, then the 20 EMA: A young listing has no 200-day, and our card does not ask for one here.

questions.simple: It needs a close above the rising 9 and 20 EMA now, and above the 50-day only once it exists.

reasons: one source: the criteria card (c22), a proposed gate

questions.q: A new issue breaks out of its base with price above its rising 9 and 20 EMA. That's the spot you want it in.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: Right. I want a breakout from strength, sitting on top of rising short averages. That tells you buyers held it up through the base. If it's stuck under them, the base is still weak. Once a 50-day exists, I want it above that too. It's too young for a 200-day, so you judge it on the lines it has.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the IPO breakout from strength, above the rising 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.simple: True. Above rising short lines means buyers held it up, so the breakout comes from strength.

reasons: one source: the criteria card (c22), a proposed gate

questions.q: You just bought an IPO breakout and you'll be watching the screen all day. A stop in your head is good enough.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: No. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker. A mental stop is a debate you have with yourself while price is falling. A real order fires on its own, even if you look away, freeze, or the stock drops fast. New issues move fast, so that matters even more. The stop is an appointment, not a debate.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False. A real stop order fires on its own, even if you look away or freeze.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
questions.story: You bought the IPO-high break at 33.38, with the stop at 32.62 under the low of the day. It's wobbling, and you're tempted to lower the stop to give it air.
choices: Leave it, or raise it later
Lower it a bit, it's a new issue
Cancel it and watch the price
Lower it, but only after a trim
questions.answer: Leave it, or raise it later
questions.why: Leave it, or raise it. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. You set 32.62 where the trade is wrong, under the breakout day's low. Lowering it doesn't make the trade better. It just turns a planned loss into a bigger one. Giving a trade air after you're in is how small losses grow. VIK held, ran to 5.1R, then rolled over. The trail did the selling.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the stop before the buy. It only goes up from there.

wrong.Lower it, but only after a trim: A trim doesn't change it. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Lower it a bit, it's a new issue: New issues get no pass. Lower the stop and you've widened the loss.
wrong.Cancel it and watch the price: A stop in your head isn't a stop. Keep the real order with the broker.

questions.simple: Leave it or raise it. The stop marks where you're wrong, and lowering it only makes a bigger loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: It's working. When does your stop come up to breakeven?
choices: Somewhere 2R to 5R, or at first sell
At 0.5R to 1R, back at the pivot
Only after the last piece is sold
After the first higher close
questions.answer: Somewhere 2R to 5R, or at first sell
questions.why: Anywhere from 2R to 5R, or when you make the first sell. Exactly where is your call. Breakeven is the line after which a winner should never turn into a loser. Move it too early and normal wiggle stops you out of a good trade. Wait for the last piece to sell and you've given a winner far too long to turn red.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven goes in somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. Where is your call.

wrong.At 0.5R to 1R, back at the pivot: Too soon. Normal wiggle takes you out. The window opens at 2R.
wrong.Only after the last piece is sold: Way too late. It comes up with the first sell or in the 2R to 5R window.
wrong.After the first higher close: One higher close is way too soon. Normal wiggle takes you out. Wait for 2R or the first sell.

questions.simple: Somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell. After that a winner should never turn into a loser.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: What price opens your breakeven window?
questions.why: 24.97. Your R here is 22.81 minus 21.73, which is 1.08 a share. The window opens at 2R, so add two of those to the fill: 22.81 plus 2 times 1.08 is 24.97. From there up to 5R, or at the first sell, the stop can come up to 22.81. Where inside that window is a judgment. Mark 2R the day you buy so you're not doing math with the stock moving.
questions.lesson_line: Mark 2R on the day you buy. That's where breakeven comes on the table.
questions.simple: 24.97. Add two times your risk a share to the fill, and that's where the window opens.

deeper.trap: 2R is where the window opens, not the required spot. The stop may also move at the first sell, which is a judgment, not a fixed 3R mark. Moving earlier leaves the trade less room, and moving later risks giving back a winner.

questions.q: What does that do to the IPO base?
questions.story: A new issue priced at $20, opened at $21 and closed its first day at $22. In week three of its base the low hits $18.60. It then closes under $19 for two weeks.
choices: It ends the base before the trigger
It is a normal shakeout; keep waiting
It resets the base to a fresh day one
It lowers the grade but the base stays
questions.answer: It ends the base before the trigger
questions.why: It ends the base before the trigger. Our card voids a base when the low undercuts the IPO price and the stock does not close back above it soon after. Here the low hit $18.60 against a $20 price, and the closes stayed under $19 for two weeks. MarketSmith India says the base should not undercut the IPO price.
questions.lesson_line: A base that sinks under the IPO price and stays there is over.

wrong.It is a normal shakeout; keep waiting: The base should not undercut the IPO price. Two weeks of closes under it is not a shakeout.
wrong.It resets the base to a fresh day one: The listing day does not move. This rest is over as an IPO base.
wrong.It lowers the grade but the base stays: A grade cue is not an end. Our card ends the base when the low undercuts the IPO price and no close gets back above it soon after.

questions.simple: It ends the base, because the low went under the IPO price and the stock never closed back above it.

deeper.trap: Three prices matter in this story: the $20 offer, the $21 open and the $22 first close. The low of $18.60 is under all three, and the closes stayed under $19, so the call does not depend on which one you count.

reasons: rests on held decisions (D-057 which price counts, D-002)

questions.q: What is the best read of it?
questions.story: A new issue falls 60% from its IPO high, then rests there for four weeks. The rest looks quiet and neat.
choices: Too deep to count as an IPO base
Too short; it needs five weeks
Fine, if you cut the size in half
Fine; volatile bases go to 50%
questions.answer: Too deep to count as an IPO base
questions.why: Too deep. IPO bases usually do not top 20%, and MarketSmith India sees up to 50% in volatile markets. A 60% fall is past both, and at 60% our card ends the base.
questions.lesson_line: Too deep is not a base, however quiet the rest looks.

wrong.Fine, if you cut the size in half: Size cannot rescue a base that is already over.
wrong.Too short; it needs five weeks: Four weeks is a normal length. IBD says IPO bases usually run two to five weeks, so length is not the problem.
wrong.Fine; volatile bases go to 50%: MarketSmith India sees up to 50% in volatile markets. A 60% fall is past even that.

questions.simple: It is too deep to be an IPO base, because most correct under 20% and even volatile markets see up to 50%.

deeper.trap: Quiet is not the same as sound. A rest can look neat on the chart and still sit on a 60% fall. Read the depth before the tidiness.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-055: the depth cap)

questions.story: Two new issues each priced at $15, opened at $15.20 and closed day one at $15.60. Weeks later, both bases dip to a low of $14.20 before any trigger. Stock A closes at $16.10 the next session. Stock B closes under $15 for the next five sessions.
questions.q: Which base does our card end before the trigger?
choices: Only B, which never got back above
Both, since each undercut the price
Neither, since no trigger has fired
Neither; undercuts just lower a grade
questions.answer: Only B, which never got back above
questions.why: Only B. Our card ends a base when the low undercuts the IPO price and does not close back above it within 3 sessions. Stock A closed at $16.10 one session after its dip. Stock B closed under $15 for five sessions, past the 3. MarketSmith India is stricter: it says the base should not undercut the IPO price at all.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, a dip under the IPO price gets 3 sessions to close back above it.
questions.simple: Only B, because our card ends a base that stays under the IPO price for more than 3 sessions.

wrong.Both, since each undercut the price: Our card gives an undercut 3 sessions to close back above the IPO price. Stock A did it in one, so this check does not end its base.
wrong.Neither, since no trigger has fired: This check runs before the trigger. A base can end before it ever breaks out.
wrong.Neither; undercuts just lower a grade: Stock B did not close back above the price within 3 sessions. On our card that ends the base.

deeper.trap: The 3-session window is our card's proposal, not a source's. MarketSmith India wants no undercut at all. Stock A's close of $16.10 sits above the offer, the open and the day-one close, so the call holds whichever one counts.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ipo.inv_ipo_price); the 3 sessions are the dossier's number
which price counts as the IPO price is held (D-057); the story clears every option on the card

questions.q: A new issue closes above its IPO AVWAP, the average price paid since listing, weighted by volume. What's that telling you?
choices: The average buyer is ahead
It has cleared its IPO high
Volume's drying up on pullbacks
The average buyer is underwater
questions.answer: The average buyer is ahead
questions.why: The average buyer is in profit. The IPO AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price from the listing day on. Think of it as what the typical share since the IPO cost. Above it, most holders are green and nobody's desperate to get out. Under it, they're underwater, and some will sell the first bounce to get even. I like a base that holds above it. It still isn't the buy. That's the trade through the IPO high.
questions.lesson_line: Above the IPO AVWAP, the average buyer since listing is in profit.

wrong.The average buyer is underwater: Backwards. Above the average price means the average buyer is ahead.
wrong.It has cleared its IPO high: The AVWAP is an average price, not the high. The pivot is still the IPO high.
wrong.Volume's drying up on pullbacks: The AVWAP uses volume to weight the price. It says nothing about pullback volume.

questions.simple: The average buyer is ahead. Most holders are in profit, so fewer are looking to sell.
